blocks.html: In discussing the sublime in the Critique of Judgment, Kant conjures up images of enormous mountains and seas, along with terrifyingly powerful overhanging cliffs, thunderstorms, and explosive volcanoes. While not explicit, such examples provided by Kant himself suggest that the notion of sublimity is fundamentally attached to nature and the feeling of a “negative pleasure” in the superiority of reason over such natural phenomena. However, even with such emphasis on the sublime in nature, Kant’s framework allows for sublimity to exist in art, especially in cinema as it relates to the dynamical sublime. This position stems from the fact that Kant’s notion of the sublime is not actually rooted in an external object — like nature — but rather in a mental development that establishes the superiority of the faculty of reason: “it is produced by the feeling of a momentary inhibition of the vital forces followed immediately by an outpouring of them that is all the stronger.”1 As such, the external object is merely a facilitator of stimulus that leads to a specific mental phenomenon that we label as the sublime, not the source of the sublime.

Thus, I will argue that Kant’s notion of the dynamical sublime can be experienced in art, specifically in film. To build the argument, I will first analyze general properties of Kantian sublimity as it relates to nature, subsequently linking it to Kant’s general remarks on aesthetic ideas and fine art, and why such ideas facilitate the experience of sublimity outside of natural phenomena, and more specifically, in cinema. To end, I will refer to an example in Christopher Nolan’s film Interstellar that exhibits the dynamical sublime, along with allusions to similar scenes from other movies.

Kant expressly rejects the view that nature itself is sublime. This rejection is the main separation that Kant makes between judgments of beauty and judgments of the sublime. Particularly, we can call natural objects beautiful, but not independently sublime, because while any judgment of beauty “carries with it a purposiveness in its form, by which the object seems as it were pre-determined for our power of judgment,” a judgment of the sublime “may indeed appear, in its form, contrapurposive for our power of judgment, incommensurate with our power of exhibition”2 In this respect, we may point to a flower or an oak tree and make a judgment that the object itself is beautiful; in the case of the sublime, we cannot point to those objects and call them sublime since “we apprehend [sublimity] as in itself contrapurposive.”3 Thus, the sublime carries a much more mental definition than beauty and cannot exhibit itself in a purely sensible or perceptual form.

The sublime “concerns only ideas of reason.”4 When an object engages the faculties of the individual’s mind — specifically, the faculties of imagination and reason — and overpowers imaginative capability, we can begin to experience the sublime. The object itself is not the source of sublimity. Rather, the sublime is a feeling of negative pleasure; a universally valid moment defined by the initial apprehension and subsequent feeling of superiority in our power of reason when understanding the incommensurate nature of an object. As Kant puts it, in such an experience, “the mind is induced to abandon sensibility and occupy itself with ideas containing a higher purposiveness.”5 This alternation between such fear and the pleasure of experiencing “ideas of reason” due to such fear is not fundamentally tied to nature — thus, “we express ourselves entirely incorrectly when we call this or that object of nature sublime.”6 It becomes clear that neither nature itself (nor art itself, for that matter) can be independently defined as sublime. Thus, Kant has left open the possibility that an aesthetic object outside of the natural objects he cites can induce the sublime, as long as it elicits the power of reason over the faculty of imagination — the negative pleasure. As such, the question now becomes whether this object can indeed be an artistic object. To fully understand this point, we have to analyze what Kant means by art, and whether it fundamentally differs from sublime nature as an object to instigate sublimity to exclude its place in Kantian theory.

Seemingly a fatal blow to the idea of sublime art is Kant’s concept of aesthetic ideas, which he first begins to outline in On the Powers of the Mind Which Constitute Genius. Such ideas are imperative to the creation of fine art: it is the “animating principle” of an artist’s mind. He states that an aesthetic idea is the “presentation of the imagination which prompts much thought, but to which no determinate thought whatsoever, i.e., no [determinate] concept can be adequate, so that no language can express it completely and allow us to grasp it.”7 Two sections later from this, Kant delivers a statement that seems to reject sublime art: “We may in general call beauty (whether natural or artistic) the expression of aesthetic ideas; the difference is that in the case of fine art the aesthetic idea must be prompted by a concept of the object.”8 Kant has defined “fine art” as the expression of an aesthetic idea, represented through an artistic object’s higher concept. However, these statements also seem to infer that such expressions of aesthetic ideas constitute beauty, not sublimity. If aesthetic ideas, and accordingly, fine art, cannot evoke the sublime and can only express beauty, it seems the argument for artistic sublimity crumbles before it even begins.

However, such a strict reading is not imposed on us by Kant. He defines aesthetic ideas to be conducive to a broad interpretation, and sensible expressions of the concept are not restricted to communicating beauty only. Namely, while an artist aims to present aesthetic ideas as a united structure that conveys beauty, it does not mean that the aesthetic idea itself is beautiful, nor does it mean that the exhibition of the idea has to be beautiful to us. To take a step back, it is clear that products of our faculty of imagination is what generates aesthetic ideas: “imagination…is very mighty when it creates…another nature out of the material that actual nature gives it…We may even restructure experience; and though in doing so we continue to follow analogical laws, yet we also follow principles which reside higher up, namely, in reason…we can process that material into something quite different.”9 In this respect, aesthetic ideas stands in contrast to rational ideas, but the two concepts are not necessarily mutually exclusive. We note that aesthetic ideas bridge the gap between our faculty of imagination and the concept of rational ideas, or ideas of reason. Specifically, aesthetic ideas seek to characterize the rational ideas that we cannot see in life; as such, aesthetic ideas are not necessarily beautiful. They can actually be quite terrifying.

Similarly, the expressions of such aesthetic ideas — what Kant calls fine art — encompasses broad presentations of the imagination that “surpasses nature,” trying to “approach an exhibition of rational concepts (intellectual ideas), and thus [these objects] are given a semblance of objective reality.”10 In other words, purely intellectual ideas like power, infinity, moral righteousness, or wickedness can be presented to us sensibly through aesthetic ideas. These are the efforts of many historically recognized artists; Iago in Giuseppe Verdi’s Otello may be thought of as the anthropomorphous representation of ruthless evil, an idea with no universal sensible expression. We may regard the opera as a beautiful work of art in considering its entire form, but the aesthetic ideas that are expressed seek to sensibly approximate rational ideas, like in Iago’s case — there exists a “concept of the object.”11 Thus, the exhibition of such aesthetic ideas are not beautiful in and of themselves. Furthermore, aesthetic ideas may also be perfect models of certain human experiences, intensified to an unattainable maximum. Kant gives the example of a poet who “takes [thingsl that are indeed exemplified in experience, such as death, envy, and all the other vices, as well as love, fame, and…by means of an imagination that emulates the example of reason…he ventures to give these sensible expression in a way that goes beyond the limits of experience, namely, with a completeness for which no example can be found in nature.”12

As such, the expression of aesthetic ideas (fine art) is not only restrained to the domain of beauty. Further, Kant’s description of fine art actually seems to have more common with his description of experiencing the sublime than it does with judging the beautiful. Remember that the sublime “concerns only ideas of reason,” and in the specific case of the dynamical sublime, “the irresistibility of nature's might makes us, considered as natural beings, recognize our physical impotence.”13 Similarly, when artists attempt to exhibit aesthetic ideas through art like poetry or painting, they process material “into something quite different, namely, into something that surpasses nature…they do at least strive toward something that lies beyond the bounds of experience.”14 These two descriptions are nearly identical; both require that a presentation of the imagination elicit a superior power of reason. Thus, the expressive power in fine art and the sublime both aim to produce aesthetic experiences that force our faculty of imagination to its absolute maximum limit, which in turn summons rational ideas that aim to interpret the sensible object that lies before us. The artist’s imagination attempts to strive beyond limits of our conventional experience and let our power of reason expand past determinate concepts, much like a powerful storm or the idea of God can impel us to recognize the overwhelming power of nature, subsequently eliciting a detached fear and our “soul's fortitude above its usual middle range and allow us to discover in ourselves an ability to resist which is of a quite different kind, and which gives us the courage [to believe] that we could be a match for nature's seeming omnipotence.”15 Aesthetic ideas are quite similar to the sublime; the expressions of the former are tied to the evocation of rational ideas, like the sublime, more so than the beautiful.

Kant’s own words demonstrate that the sublime is not tied a natural object, and furthermore, that expressions of aesthetic ideas — specifically, fine art — are not tied to the domain of beauty. More specifically, just as the sublime concerns the superiority of ideas of reason, fine art, through expressing aesthetic ideas, also concerns the exhibition of ideas of reason over imagination. Thus, he leaves open the possibility that art can indeed provoke the judgment of sublimity, since art itself can simulate exhibiting indeterminate concepts. However, we still cannot say that sublime art exists just because Kant does not preclude the mere possibility of an object outside of nature invoking a sublime experience, nor can we say that sublime art exists simply because the underlying principle governing fine art — the expression of aesthetic ideas — strives to stimulate the same faculties of mind and may induce a similar experience to that of the sublime. To say that the sublime can be found in art imposes a stricter understanding of the art itself. There must be attributes within the fine art that induces the specific mental movement of the sublime; it is not enough that the object of the art may constitute sublime content, like a hurricane or God’s power.

Specifically, the fine art must aesthetically characterize objects such that it sets the audience’s “power of intellectual ideas (i.e. reason) in motion,” where we can consider the expression of the aesthetic idea itself as sublime “insofar as [it] present[s] unboundedness, either [as] in the object or because the object prompts us to present it.”16 As we have seen, fine art is created by an artist’s imagination, and Kant expressly states that there are presentations of an individual’s imagination “such that, even though this presentation belongs to the exhibition of the concept [rational ideas], yet it prompts, even by itself, so much thought as can never be comprehended within a determinate concept and thereby the presentation aesthetically expands the concept itself in an unlimited way.”17 While succeeding at creating such artwork is difficult, as it attempts to emulate ideas that inherently escape normal powers of exhibition, a successful execution describes an almost exact explanation of how Kant details nature as inducing the sublime.

But the question now becomes: is there actually sublime fine art in the world? The constraints are excruciatingly tight. For an artist to create a piece of work that can be considered sublime, he must (1) ensure a presentation of his imagination that (2) exhibits an aesthetic idea and through an object, (3) attempts to sensibly express a rational concept that (4) exists beyond the realms of normal experience and nature (unboundedness). Only then, can an artwork possibly be an “exhibition of an indeterminate concept of reason,” which is what Kant regards the sublime as.18 Such constraints are the reason Kant only explored nature as an object suitable for exhibiting sublimity, because “the sublime in art is always confined to the conditions that [art] must meet to be in harmony with nature.”19 Essentially, it is easier to find the sublime in nature, because it “arouses in us, merely in apprehension and without any reasoning on our part, a feeling of the sublime,” while fine art must first meet the requirements of fine art before we can even begin considering it to be sublime.20 Nevertheless, he does not preclude fine art from the realm of inducing the sublimity found in the mind, and one form of artistic work seems to most easily meet the requirements: cinema.

I will restrict myself to a discussion of cinema in the context of the dynamical sublime, because a consideration of cinema in the mathematical sublime leads to arguments about how one watches film rather than the film itself. Since the dynamical sublime depends on a fear of an object that stems from power, we may more easily speak about the contents of the movie (i.e. the actual artwork), whereas the mathematical sublime is concerned with infinite magnitudes, and the medium through which you watch the movie would affect whether you could potentially derive a sublime experience from it (i.e. watching the same film on IMAX vs. a small computer screen. The former is more conducive to mathematically sublime experiences, while the latter would not be, even when watching the same film).

The most immediate example of a piece of artwork inducing a sublimity that forces us to “abandon sensibility and occupy itself with ideas containing a higher purposiveness” is a scene depicting a gravity slingshot around a black hole in Christopher Nolan’s Interstellar.21 The film confronts a challenge: conveying the incredible dynamic power of a black hole to the audience and the actions our scientists must take to overcome its force and save the human race. We intimately observe the black hole’s immense gravitational pull warping light, space, and time from the top of the frame to the bottom of the frame, using the vertical axis to show the massive energy this celestial body holds. It bends the very fabric of spacetime, pulling clouds of lightness and darkness rhythmically downwards. This vertical orientation of the black hole relative to the screen not only serves as a visceral representation of the hyperkinetic force, but it also becomes the referential object that our protagonists must overcome.22

In such a presentation of Nolan’s imagination, we encounter an aesthetic idea. The director aims to visually depict a phenomena that quite literally is infinite in mass and density, exhibiting a natural force that, as one of the scientists in the film puts it, “sucks in comets and asteroids and planets.” We would not be able to comprehend its power through mere language; during the time of the film’s production, an image of a black hole had never even been captured before. The scene epitomizes an attempt to sensibly express an utterly terrifying rational concept that not only possesses infinite destructive power, but also (at the time) existed only as a mathematical equation — beyond the scope of anybody’s experience. The aesthetic experience itself calls forth a greater apprehension if and recognition for multiple rational concepts in the scene: infinite power, ultimate destruction, the powerlessness of a human confronted with such a power, a fear of failure, among others. Ultimately, the sublimity is derived from reason’s domination over our fear, personified by our protagonists’ attempt to overcome the power of the black hole; as such, the scene induces the sublime not because it “arouses fear, but because it calls forth our strength.”23 The cinematic medium facilities a viewing of such maximal phenomena from a position of safety, removed from being actively fearful of the black hole or the near-impossible challenge that our protagonists face.

Nolan effectively forces us to recognize the overwhelming power of a black hole, which elicits our detached fear of a natural phenomenon through our relationships to the cinematic viewing experience and the narrative we have seen so far. In this respect, this scene fulfills the requirement of sublime art; Nolan engages his faculty of imagination to express an indeterminate concept through sensible means, attempting to approximate the fear of an infinite power in the form of a black hole, subsequently stimulating the viewer’s disinterested fear through the screen. We are pushed to think “of the case where we might possibly want to put up resistance against it, and that any resistance would in that case be utterly futile,” effectively overpowering our imagination with our power of reason and the consideration of rational ideas, thus instigating the dynamically sublime through such a mental movement grounded in fear and awe.

Experiencing sublimity is not exclusive to purely natural phenomena. While finding the sublime in art is a much more difficult process and is bound to be rare, such experiences to exist in reality. Interstellar’s black hole scene is just one instantiation; the “God Storm Scene” in Ang Lee’s The Life of Pi and the “worm scene” in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune are two more examples of a director stimulating an audience’s detached fear of natural power through artwork and invoking the higher faculty of reason to the mind’s foreground.24 Kant shows that judgments of the sublime are not inherently rooted in natural phenomena; aesthetic ideas also seek to prompt rational thought about indeterminate concepts, just as the sublime does. Exhibitions of aesthetic ideas — labelled as fine art — are the apt presentation of such aesthetic ideas by an artist’s imagination, prompted by a concept of the artistically depicted object. Thus, when a film, like Nolan’s Interstellar, Lee’s The Life of Pi, or Villeneuve’s Dune can exhibit aesthetic ideas through a concept of an object and calls forth the superiority of the viewer’s power of reason through disinterested fear, dynamically sublime art has effectively been created. While our protagonists face the fear associated with the power of nature, we, as the audience, possess the luxury to both be in fear of the scene and understand its higher purposiveness in the context of the film, all by using our supersensible faculty of reason.
The essay’s three appendices are film stills from Interstellar, Life of Pi and Dune. They are left out of this web version.

notes: Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Judgment, §49, 314 (pg. 182) (emphasis added)
